content: The 2019 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services include a detailed analysis of the cost-effectiveness of maternal HIV retesting in both highand low-HIV burden settings. This analysis, conducted by Julianne Meisner and colleagues, utilized Markov models to evaluate the health and economic impacts of maternal HIV retesting on mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV in four countries: Kenya and South Africa (high/intermediate HIV prevalence) and Colombia and Ukraine (low HIV prevalence). The study assessed five retesting scenarios, varying in frequency from late pregnancy through nine months postpartum, and compared these strategies using incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) against a cost-effectiveness threshold of 50% of the gross domestic product (GDP). The findings revealed that in high HIV burden settings, such as Kenya and South Africa, retesting once during late pregnancy with follow-up testing through six weeks postpartum was cost-effective. This strategy reduced infant HIV infections attributable to new maternal infections by 24% in Kenya (ICER = $241 per disability-adjusted life year [DALY] averted) and 21% in South Africa (ICER = $572 per DALY averted). Adding one or two additional postpartum retests provided marginal benefits, averting 2–4% more infections, but adding three retests during the postpartum period resulted in higher benefits (5–8% more infections averted) at significantly higher costs, with ICERs exceeding the cost-effectiveness threshold ($7,820 in Kenya and $10,463 in South Africa). In low HIV burden settings, such as Colombia and Ukraine, all retesting strategies exceeded the cost-effectiveness threshold and prevented relatively few infant infections (up to 33 in Colombia and 5 in Ukraine). This lack of cost-effectiveness was attributed to the low HIV prevalence and low breastfeeding rates among HIV-positive mothers in these countries. The study concluded that in high HIV burden settings, a single retest during late pregnancy is the most cost-effective strategy for preventing infant HIV infections. Adding one or two postpartum tests marginally reduced MTCT and was less costly than adding three retests. In contrast, retesting in low HIV burden settings was not cost-effective at any time point due to the low prevalence of HIV and limited breastfeeding among HIV-positive mothers.
